notes.1a: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates correctly identified the instrument in Figure 1.1 as a Barometer. [Limited responses] • Some answers incorrectly named the instrument as a Pressure Gauge or Pressure Meter. • Many candidates wrote incorrect versions of Barometer for example Barometre, Baremotre. �PAGE�20
notes.1aii: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates were aware that ‘mb’ represented ‘millibars’ as the unit of pressure measurement. [Limited responses] • Quite a few candidates misunderstood the question and gave answers that were not related to ‘mb’. ‘Pascals’ was a common incorrect answer; while it is a unit of pressure, it is not represented by ‘mb’.
notes.1iii: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates recognised that they needed to plot a continuous line and a dashed line to demarcate the minimum temperature trend from the maximum temperate trend. • Many candidates recognised that they needed to plot the two temperatures with crosses on the correct date of 14 September. [Limited responses] • Some candidates did not recognise that there were two different types of line so often made both lines continuous. • Some candidates accurately plotted the top maximum temperature at 14 °C. They then misplotted the second minimum temperature at 11 °C.
notes.1b: (i) Comprehensive responses • Responses judged that the chosen anemometer was superior to the other one and gave the reason which was that it gave more accurate or detailed readings and that it was easier to read. [Limited responses] • Some responses related to the cost of the instruments, their reliability and that their choice was easier to use.
notes.1bii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates stated the advantages of using a digital anemometer such as it was easy to read or use, that it was more accurate and that it gave quicker readings. [Limited responses] • Candidates should state that a digital anemometer is likely to reduce the number of mistakes in reading, rather than eliminate them entirely.
notes.1c: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates focused on the use of the max-min thermometer shown in Figure 1.3 and stated that it was put in a Stevenson Screen, that the left side measured the minimum temperature and that the right side measured the maximum temperature. • Candidates were often aware that the temperatures were read at the bottom of the indices and that a magnet was used to reset the indices every day. [Limited responses] • Some candidates described how the instrument worked rather how it is used.
notes.1d: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates accurately plotted the two points on the graph with a cross as required. [Limited responses] • Some candidates did not accurately locate the plot at 49 which required judgement in the space between lines. • A few candidates located the second plot at 48 instead of 49; a few did not plot the second plot. �PAGE�21
notes.1dii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates made the judgement that the hypothesis was false and then added that there was no correlation between atmospheric pressure increasing and wind speed decreasing based on data in Table 1.1 and the graph plots on Figure 1.4. • Most candidates used the data in Table 1.1 to support their decision citing that there were days when the atmospheric pressure increased and wind speed increased or that there were days when one variable stayed the same while the other changed. [Limited responses] • Some candidates judged that the scatter of points on the graph Figure 1.4 did indicate that the negative relationship stated in the hypothesis was true or partially true and then continued to choose specific data to prove this. • A few candidates made the hypothesis decision and noted that there was no correlation. They did not then choose the right data to support this for example they made erroneous judgements from the graph or mixed up the days when quoting data from Table 1.1.
notes.1iv: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates did identify 20 September had the smallest daily range of temperature at 1 °C between 13 °C minimum and 14 °C maximum. [Limited responses] • Some candidates identified the lowest/smallest minimum temperature on 13 September and gave that date instead. • Some candidates gave the temperature difference of 1 °C without giving the actual temperature difference.
notes.1v: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates indicated that the hypothesis should be true. • Some candidates indicated that the hypothesis should be partially true. This was borne out as there were a few places where minimum temperature fell when maximum temperature rose and vice versa though not enough to make the hypothesis false. • Candidates decided the hypothesis was true identified that there was, a clear positive trend whereby when the maximum temperature increased, so did minimum temperature and vice- versa. They chose continuous dates and paired data to confirm this. [Limited responses] • Some candidates indicated that the hypothesis should be false and tried to support their view with the limited data that supported this hypothesis.
notes.1e: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates realised that measuring the three weather variables over a month instead of 15 days would provide them with more data or a wider range of data and give them more evidence to identify trends or patterns which would also help to eliminate anomalies. [Limited responses] • Some candidates stated that, by collecting more data, their conclusions would be more accurate which is a vague conclusion and not necessarily true. More data does not equal more accuracy. • Some candidates judged that an average could be calculated for a month instead of 15 days without understanding that would not make results more reliable. �PAGE�22
notes.1eii: Comprehensive responses • Candidates suggested that measuring the weather variables at different times of the year would allow comparisons and indicate similarities and differences due to seasonal effects, giving more justifiable conclusions than those obtained over a few weeks. [Limited responses] • Some candidates gave generic answers such as the results would make conclusions more accurate or that an average could be calculated; neither would make the conclusions more reliable.
notes.1f: Comprehensive responses • Many candidates could suggest a worthwhile hypothesis to extend their weather fieldwork. • Candidates came up with either a question for example, ‘Does rainfall increase when temperature decreases?’, or a statement for example, ‘Atmospheric pressure increases when rainfall is low.’ to investigate collecting rainfall data. • Candidates realised that it was only required to answer a description of the fieldwork method to collect rainfall data not the other variable in their hypothesis. • Responses included using a rain gauge in an open area with its top just above the ground to collect rainfall. Other answers could include checking the amount by pouring the water into a measuring cylinder and reading off the scale the amount of rainfall in millimetres and then; after emptying the rain gauge, it would be reset for the next 24-hour period. [Limited responses] • Some candidates did not realise what a hypothesis was. They suggested topics such as ‘Rainfall during the day’ or ‘Temperature and Rainfall’. • Some candidates did suggest an appropriate hypothesis but did not elaborate as to how to collect rainfall data. • Responses such as collect the rainfall data when it’s raining or measure rainfall only on days when it rains demonstrates a need for more understanding of the fieldwork method. • Some candidates gave answers which described how to collect data from the non-rainfall variable for example how to measure temperature or pressure.
notes.2a: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates correctly stated that the initials CBD stood for Central Business District. [Limited responses] • Some candidates thought the initials stood for Central Building Department, Central Bus Depot or Central Business Development.
notes.2aii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates correctly chose the bus station as the land use most likely to be in the CBD of a town. [Limited responses] • Instead of choosing the bus station, some candidates thought that other land uses, especially the airport or a factory, were more likely to be in the CBD.
notes.2b: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates correctly named an appropriate sampling method such as random, systematic or stratified. • Random sampling was chosen by many candidates describing the method by suggesting that any person could be asked or that a system using a random number generator for taking numbers from a hat could be used. • Systematic sampling was chosen by many candidates stating that it required choosing people at regular or equal intervals and giving an example such as every nineth or tenth person. • Stratified sampling method was chosen by a minority of candidates suggesting that the sample selected would be based on grouping people by reference to age and/or gender. [Limited responses] �PAGE�23 0460 Geography March 2026 • Some candidates suggested sampling methods that were not appropriate methods such as quantitative methods, questionnaires, surveys or interviews. • Some candidates chose the random method and then did not elaborate further. • Some candidates that chose the systematic method referred to people being chosen at intervals rather than ‘regular’ intervals. A few suggested choosing every second person which is too frequent to be called sampling. • Stratified sampling requires a sample to be chosen that relates to the total population. While candidates were aware it related to age and gender, candidates needed to state that the sample would be chosen related to the socio-economic data of the whole population. • Some candidates explained their choice suggesting that it gave every person an equal chance of being picked or that it avoided bias.
notes.2bii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates suggested two appropriate problems students might have while using the questionnaire. The most popular answers included people not wanting to answer, being too busy or being suspicious of the motives. • Candidates were aware that not everybody the students asked would have visited the supermarket or that they might be a visitor so they could not answer the questionnaire. Language issues was also a problem that was raised. [Limited responses] • Some candidates suggested that people being questioned might lie or deliberately give incorrect answers. This is not a problem with using the questionnaire as the students would never know. • Some candidates suggested that it would be time-consuming or that the answers might be vague. As the questionnaire in Figure 2.2 involved only circling four choices, there could be no vague answers, and it would take very little time to complete.
notes.2c: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates plotted both lines accurately and correctly shaded in the three sections. [Limited responses] • Some candidates only plotted one line accurately, usually the 91 plot. • A small number of candidates reversed the plotting and shading. • A few candidates did not attempt the graph completion.
notes.2cii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates correctly judged that the hypothesis was true and supported that decision by making a statement that over half, the most or the majority of questionnaire results showed that, for three of the four statements, most responses strongly agreed and agreed with the hypothesis. • Most candidates also provided data from the table that supported the hypothesis for example 64 people strongly agreed and agreed that the supermarket provided more choice of goods. [Limited responses] • Some candidates incorrectly suggested that the hypothesis was partially true or even false as they placed too much emphasis on the fourth statement which showed 49 people agreed that it had cheaper prices and 51 disagreed. These figures were too close to justify a partial response and the data for the other three statements clearly supported the hypothesis. • Some candidates’ data evidence involved adding up the columns instead of reading along the rows.
notes.2d: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates correctly stated that the student scores for agree and disagree were 75 and 76. �PAGE�24 0460 Geography March 2026 [Limited responses] • A few candidates did not attempt this question.
notes.2dii: Comprehensive responses • Almost all candidates drew the bar accurately at 260. [Limited responses] • A few candidates incorrectly drew the bar at 160 as they misread the scale. • A small number of candidates did not attempt the plot.
notes.2iii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates focused their answers on standing in a safe place as a difficulty and gave reasons why counting vehicles might be hard including that they were going too fast, traffic congestion was high and that, on wide roads, some vehicles could be hidden behind others which is very likely from their experiences in India’s urban areas. Deciding on the type of vehicle for example lorry or van might be difficult too. • Many candidates did recognise that standing for 30 minutes where there was high traffic congestion could cause breathing difficulties and that weather extremes such as heavy rain and heat could cause practical and health issues such as sunstroke. [Limited responses] • Some candidates gave vague answers such as the traffic being hard to count without reasons as to why this could be the case. Recording the same vehicle twice was also an unlikely difficulty as was the idea that the survey was time-consuming or that it would take a long time. • A few candidates focused their answer on what difficulties the survey might cause them. They suggested that it would be too noisy to concentrate, that they might get headaches or that it would be tiring and they would get bored.
notes.2e: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates suggested that, if the students were working as a group, they could discuss their scores, agree on a score or that they could take the average or most common score to overcome the issue of subjectivity. • Several candidates also suggested that it might be beneficial, for consistency, if just one person in the group was nominated to decide the score. • Most candidates suggested that the issue of the score being at different times of day could be overcome by either requiring that the scores were all taken at the same time of day or by taking an average. [Limited responses] • In the second part of this question, some candidates suggested taking the score at different times of day which was the issue that they needed to overcome. The problem was that the score had been taken at different times of day.
notes.2eii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates did use the ruler to draw a bar accurately at -4 (20 mm) using the start line provided. [Limited responses] • Some candidates drew bars below or above the 20 mm length required. • Some candidates drew a 20 mm bar accurately above the provided line instead of below it to clarify at +4 instead of -4.
notes.2f: (i) Comprehensive responses • Most candidates identified ‘tally’ as the method to use with the recording sheet. [Limited responses] • A small number of candidates incorrectly chose ‘estimate’ as the way to complete the recording sheet. �PAGE�25
notes.2fii: Comprehensive responses • Most candidates gave detailed descriptions of how they would carry out the traffic count. • Most common responses involved working in groups or pairs, dividing tasks up between the group such as counting different types of vehicles and counting on different sides of the road. • Some responses suggested using a timer and a counter/tally to record the count and noted the importance of carrying out the count at the same time at all sites for comparative purposes. [Limited responses] • Candidates did not suggest circling the location as part of the survey method. • Some candidates also suggested carrying out the count at several times in the day for a fixed period such as 10 minutes or even an hour. The recording sheet stated the three times the survey would be carried out and that each of these times was a fixed period of 30 minutes. • Some candidates thought a traffic count involved using a questionnaire with people who were driving vehicles. • A few candidates decided that a traffic count involved counting people and their answer focused almost entirely on carrying out pedestrian counts.
notes.key_messages:
• Most candidates attempted the graph and table completions successfully although a minority did not
attempt some of these practical questions.
• Most candidates did make the correct decisions about the hypotheses they were asked to make
judgements on.
What candidates did well
• In Question 1 most candidates recognised the types of weather instruments used such as the
barometer in Question 1(a)(i).
• Most candidates gave two correct advantages of using a digital anemometer to measure wind speed.
• In Question 1(d)(i) most candidates plotted the two points and the temperature lines correctly; the
majority also chose 20 September as the correct date with the smallest temperature range.
• In Question 2, most candidates demonstrated a good grasp of geographical terminology particularly
with terms such as Central Business District in Question 2(a)(i).
• Most candidates attempted graph and table completions accurately for example Question 2(c)(i), (d)
and (f)(i) which required a demonstration of several different practical skills.
What candidates needed to improve
• In Question 1 some candidates did not know the names of instruments used in measuring weather
variables for example Question 1(a)(i) barometers measure air pressure not pressure gauges or
• A large number of candidates did not know that, in Question 1(a)(ii) the abbreviation ‘mb’ stood for
‘millibars’ as a measure of the unit of pressure.
• Many candidates were unaware of how some weather instruments are used for example the moveable
pointer and the measuring hand on an anemometer in Question 1(a)(iii) and how the max-min
thermometer measured temperatures Question 1(c).
• While some candidates made correct judgements about hypotheses, their decisions did not always
include a statement and supportive data taken from the resources they had been directed to.
• In Question 2 some candidates did not show a clear understanding of land use in the CBD for example
Question 2(a)(ii) where a minority did not choose the Bus Station.
• While many candidates knew a sampling method to use with the questionnaire in Question 2(b)(i), only
a few could describe the method well – usually the Systematic or Random method – not the Stratified
• A few candidates did not attempt some of the graph completions or tables where a choice needed
making such as Questions 1(d)(i), (iii), (c)(i), Question 2(d)(ii) and (e)(iii).
